To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the spinal cords of monkeys can support stepping, (2) the spinal cords are not as capable as those of other species of supporting stepping, and (3) the spinal cord is more capable than previously reported of supporting stepping.

1) monkeys with partial spinal lesions can show locomotion, 2) the locomotion is not always symmetric, and 3) the locomotor movements of monkeys with partial spinal cords are qualitatively similar to those of normal monkeys.

(1) 5 of 10 monkeys with T8 lesions showed some recovery of locomotor movements, (2) 4 of the animals exhibited unilateral hind limb steps and 1 showed bilateral hind limb stepping, and (3) 2 of the animals with unilateral hind limb stepping showed increased cycle durations of the hind limb and reduced cycle durations of the forelimb.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the recovery of locomotion after a partial spinal cord transection (T8) in rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta).
the neural mechanisms underlying locomotion and with the effects of spinal cord lesions on the organization and recovery of locomotor behavior in primates.
the study of the neural mechanisms underlying the recovery of motor function following injury to the nervous system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the primate's locomotor system is not as well organized as that of the rat or cat.
the primate's ability to recover locomotor movements is not significantly less than that of other mammals, and that a complete transection of the primate spinal cord is an unusual occurrence.
the monkey's spinal cord is not essential for the initiation of locomotor movements but is important for the maintenance of normal interlimb phase relationships.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, although the monkey spinal cord seems less capable than other mammals' of readily organizing locomotion, it can nevertheless organize some locomotor movements in the presence of very significant lesions.
the primate's ability to organize locomotor movements is more dependent on supraspinal influences than that of other mammals.
although the spinal cord of monkeys is capable of producing locomotion, it requires the participation of the brainstem and/or the cortex to do so.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in contrast with the findings in rats, cats, and dogs, primates with complete spinal cord transection are not able to generate locomotion.
, while the spinal cord is not essential for locomotion in primates, the spinal cord is necessary for normal locomotion.
the spinal cord of the primate is capable of generating locomotor-like movements, even in the presence of a very severe lesion.
